title: Explain Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, and when each is used.
shortTitle: Explain Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, and when each is used

s1_definition.profdef: These are four creational design patterns that each solve a different object-construction problem. Factory Method defines a method that decides which concrete class to instantiate, letting subclasses or configuration choose the product. Abstract Factory produces whole families of related objects without naming their concrete classes. Builder constructs a complex object step by step, avoiding huge constructors. Prototype creates new objects by cloning an existing instance rather than constructing from scratch.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Factory Method is the single counter that hands you the right account-opening kit based on the type you ask for. Abstract Factory is the regional office that hands you a whole matching set — forms, card design, and cheque book — for a given region, so everything is consistent. Builder is how you fill a long loan application one field at a time and only submit when it is complete. Prototype is photocopying a standard pre-filled template form and tweaking a couple of fields instead of writing the whole form again.
s1_definition.oneliner: Factory Method picks one product, Abstract Factory picks a matching family, Builder assembles one complex product step by step, and Prototype copies an existing product.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are four creational design patterns that each solve a different object-construction problem. Factory Method defines a method that decides which concrete class to instantiate, letting subclasses or configuration choose the product. Abstract Factory produces whole families of related objects without naming their concrete classes. Builder constructs a complex object step by step, avoiding huge constructors. Prototype creates new objects by cloning an existing instance rather than constructing from scratch.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Factory Method is the single counter that hands you the right account-opening kit based on the type you ask for. Abstract Factory is the regional office that hands you a whole matching set — forms, card design, and cheque book — for a given region, so everything is consistent. Builder is how you fill a long loan application one field at a time and only submit when it is complete. Prototype is photocopying a standard pre-filled template form and tweaking a couple of fields instead of writing the whole form again.

**One line to remember:** Factory Method picks one product, Abstract Factory picks a matching family, Builder assembles one complex product step by step, and Prototype copies an existing product.

sections.s2_technical:
Factory Method centralizes the decision of which concrete class to create behind a method. The caller asks for a product by a key and never writes `new`. For example `SettlementStrategy s = SettlementFactory.create(TradeType.EQUITY)` returns an EquitySettlement. You use it when you have one product hierarchy and the choice of concrete type depends on input or configuration. It satisfies Open/Closed because adding a type means adding a class and one switch branch.

Abstract Factory goes one level up: it creates families of related products that must be used together. Imagine a `ReportKitFactory` that produces a matching `Header`, `Footer`, and `Formatter` for either a regulatory report or a customer statement. For example `ReportKitFactory f = new RegulatoryKitFactory(); Header h = f.header(); Formatter fm = f.formatter();` guarantees the header and formatter belong to the same family. You use it when objects must be consistent as a set and you want to swap the whole set at once.

Builder solves the telescoping-constructor problem where a class has many fields, some optional. Instead of a constructor with ten parameters, you chain setters and call build: `Trade t = Trade.builder().tradeId("TRD-1").symbol("RELIANCE").quantity(100).price(new BigDecimal("2450")).build()`. Each call returns the builder so you can chain, and build produces an immutable object. You use it when construction has many optional parameters or when you want the result to be immutable and readable.

Prototype creates a new object by copying an existing one. When building a fresh object is expensive or you want a pre-configured template, you clone. For example a standard `OrderTemplate` with default fee and exchange can be cloned and lightly modified per order: `Order o = template.copy(); o.setQuantity(100)`. In Java this is often done with a copy constructor or a `copy()` method rather than the error-prone `Cloneable`. You use it when objects share most of their state and construction is costly or repetitive.

A senior nuance: Factory Method and Abstract Factory are about which type to create, while Builder and Prototype are about how a single object is assembled or copied. Modern Java often replaces Factory Method with a `Map<Key, Supplier<Product>>` and Prototype with a copy constructor, because these are simpler and clearer than the classic forms.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's trading platform needs all four creational patterns for different real reasons.

Problem 1 — Choosing a settlement handler. A trade arrives tagged EQUITY or FX, and the system must create the matching handler. Writing new everywhere spreads the decision across the codebase. This is exactly Factory Method: one place decides the concrete handler.

Problem 2 — Producing a consistent report kit. A regulatory report needs a regulatory header, regulatory footer, and regulatory formatter that all match; mixing a customer header with a regulatory formatter would be wrong. This is exactly Abstract Factory: one factory produces a matching family.

Problem 3 — Building a trade order with many fields. An order has an id, symbol, quantity, price, account, fee, and optional notes. A seven-argument constructor is unreadable and error-prone. This is exactly Builder: assemble the order step by step and build an immutable object.

Problem 4 — Reusing a standard order template. Most orders share the same exchange and default fee, so creating each from scratch repeats work. This is exactly Prototype: clone a pre-filled template and change only what differs.

The demo wires a Factory for handlers, an Abstract Factory for report kits, a Builder for orders, and a Prototype template that gets cloned for Rajesh's order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a trade type EQUITY, a regulatory report request, an order for RELIANCE, and a standard NSE order template cloned for TCS.

Step 1: `SettlementFactory.create(EQUITY)` runs. The factory reads the enum and returns a new EquitySettlement. The caller holds a SettlementStrategy reference and never knew the concrete class name. This is Factory Method producing one product.

Step 2: A RegulatoryKitFactory is created and asked for its header, footer, and formatter. All three belong to the same regulatory family, so there is no risk of mixing a customer header with a regulatory formatter. This is Abstract Factory producing a matching family.

Step 3: Order.builder() starts an empty builder. Each chained call sets one field and returns the builder, so the data accumulates inside the builder object step by step. No partial Order exists yet.

Step 4: build() validates that required fields are present, then constructs one immutable Order from the accumulated builder state. The order now holds id ORD-1001, symbol RELIANCE, quantity 100, price 2450.50, and fee 50.00.

Step 5: A standard OrderTemplate for NSE with a default fee rate is created once. This is the prototype that holds shared defaults.

Step 6: template.copy() runs the copy constructor, producing a brand-new OrderTemplate carrying the same exchange and fee rate. Then the clone's symbol is set to TCS and quantity to 25.

Step 7: Both objects are logged. The clone shows TCS and 25 while the original template is unchanged, proving the copy is independent. Each of the four patterns produced an object in its own way.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Factory produced: EquitySettlement
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Kit header=RBI-REGULATORY-HEADER formatter=XBRL-FORMATTER
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Built order: ORD-1001 SAV2001 RELIANCE x100 @2450.50 fee=50.00
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Prototype clone: NSE rate=0.0010 sym=TCS qty=25 (original unchanged: NSE rate=0.0010 sym=null qty=0)
```

```

    │
    ├─ FACTORY METHOD
    │    SettlementFactory.create(EQUITY) → EquitySettlement
    │
    ├─ ABSTRACT FACTORY
    │    RegulatoryKitFactory → {header, footer, formatter}  (matching family)
    │
    ├─ BUILDER
    │    Order.builder().orderId().symbol()....build()
    │      step 1 → step 2 → ... → immutable Order

    └─ PROTOTYPE

    │

  Output: 4 objects created, each via a different creational pattern
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, and Prototype are four creational patterns, and each one solves a different construction problem, so the key is knowing when to use which.

Factory Method defines a single method that decides which concrete class to instantiate, so the caller asks for a product by a key and never writes new. I use it when I have one product hierarchy and the concrete choice depends on input or configuration, for example picking an equity or FX settlement handler based on the trade type. It also supports Open/Closed because adding a new type means adding a class and one branch.

Abstract Factory goes a level higher and produces whole families of related objects that must be used together. I use it when a set of objects has to stay consistent, for example a regulatory report that needs a matching header, footer, and formatter, where mixing a customer header with a regulatory formatter would be wrong. One factory hands back the entire matching set, and swapping to a customer-statement factory swaps the whole family at once.

Builder solves the telescoping-constructor problem. When an object has many fields, some optional, a constructor with eight or ten parameters is unreadable and easy to get wrong. The Builder lets me set fields by name through chained calls and then call build to produce an immutable object, which is exactly how I construct a trade order with its id, symbol, quantity, price, and fee. Prototype creates a new object by cloning an existing one, which I use when construction is expensive or when most objects share the same baseline, for example a standard NSE order template that I copy and then tweak the symbol and quantity for each order. In modern Java I usually implement Prototype with a copy constructor rather than the error-prone Cloneable interface.

The senior point I add is that Factory Method and Abstract Factory answer which type to create, while Builder and Prototype answer how a single object is assembled or copied. In practice I also know these often simplify in modern Java, so Factory Method frequently becomes a map of keys to suppliers, and that pragmatic judgment is what the interviewer is really listening for.
